Welcome

Learn to hear the bahr

In Urdu poetry, a bahr is the underlying rhythmic pattern that an entire ghazal adheres to — a sequence of long and short syllables. This app teaches you to hear it, see it, and scan it for yourself.

How to read the marks

Every scan marks each syllable long (=, two letters) or short (–, one letter), and a flexible syllable (x) may go either way, as the meter needs. These are Pritchett’s terms (Handbook §1.5 ↗). Here is the key, and one line marked out:

flexible
A syllable in a word that can scan long or short, like ہے or میں. The meter of the line decides.
x
The same idea in a meter pattern: a slot in the bahr itself where either weight is allowed. A flexible syllable fills it.
extra
One short syllable the meter doesn’t count, allowed at a line’s end. It is left out of the pattern.

Words we use

miṣraʿ
A single line or hemistich of poetry.
sheʿr
A complete, self-contained two-line couplet.
baḥr
The meter or rhythmic pattern that a poem follows.
rukn
A metrical foot (e.g. mafāʿīlun, fāʿilātun).
flexible
A syllable that may be scanned long or short, marked x.
dum / da
Vocal mnemonics for long (=) and short (–) syllables.

Weight

How long each syllable is — the raw material of every meter.

What weight is

Every syllable is long (=) or short (–), and a meter is a pattern of them. To read a line, split each word into syllables and weigh each one.

The rules

Rule one: a syllable is two letters or one. Count letters, not sounds: every letter of the alphabet, the doubled letter a tashdīd stands for, the madd on Alif (Alif Madd, آ), and a hamza inside a word.

More: what meter ignores

Invisible to meter: the marks zer, zabar, pesh and jazm (script §5 ↗); the aspiration ھ (do-chashmī he, §10 ↗); the nasal ں (nūn-e ghunnah, §9 ↗); the dotless ی that carries a hamza. Older texts write plain gol he for aspiration; it is still invisible when it aspirates. A written jazm over a consonant says it has no vowel of its own, so it closes a syllable.

A nasalizing ن can also sit in the middle of a word. It usually comes after a long vowel; the exceptions are mostly Indic verbs with ن in the first syllable.

Handbook §1.2 ↗

The weight law. Two letters → long (=). One letter → short (–). A long is meant to last about double a short. A syllable that may go either way is called flexible.

Handbook §1.5 ↗

Rule two: begin with a consonant if you can. Every letter counts as a consonant except Alif (ا) and Alif Madd (آ), which are always vowels, and و, ی, ے when they are the second letter of a syllable. Syllables that begin with Alif (ا) or Alif Madd (آ) normally occur only at the start of a word. ع and a hamza inside a word act as consonants; a hamza is never the second letter of a syllable.

Handbook §1.3 ↗

Rule three: the split follows pronunciation. Use the ordinary spoken word, not the spelling alone; when unsure, ask a native speaker or check a dictionary that marks pronunciation.

Handbook §1.4 ↗

Flexible syllables

Some syllables can be long or short. The meter of the line decides which.

Short words

Small words like ہے and میں can go either way. Many common one-syllable words (کو، سے، کا، ہے، میں، بھی، نے، ہوں، یہ، وہ، جو، تو, and also دو، تھا، ہی، سا، سی، کے، کی، ہو، یوں) are flexible: two letters, so normally long, but the poet may scan them short. Once the meter of a line is known, each one is simply long or short there. The form is consonant + vowel or consonant + h; particles, pronouns, postpositions and verb forms are the likeliest to bend. When in doubt, treat every such one-syllable word as flexible on a first reading.

Handbook §2.1 ↗

Words that do not bend. تا، گو، یا are virtually always long; so are کیا، کیوں، جیوں (one long syllable despite the cluster) and Arabic or Persian noun monosyllables such as mai, jaa, juu. In modern usage بہ، کہ، نہ are always short (Mir sometimes scans kih and nah long).

Handbook §2.1 ↗

The word اور (aur). A special case that is a common source of error: it is scanned (= –) as two syllables or (=) as one.

Handbook §2.1 ↗

Longer words

Word endings can bend too. Inside longer words, flexibility is almost always at the end. A final two-letter syllable ending in ی, ے or ہ is nearly always flexible; one ending in و or alif often is (more in Indic verb forms than in Persian or Arabic words). Exceptions in the middle of a word are rare (koī = x x). As a rule of thumb, treat every final consonant + vowel (or consonant + h) syllable as flexible until the meter says otherwise.

Handbook §2.2 ↗

Words that can split two ways. Some consonant-heavy words may be divided in two ways: barhaman (= – =) or (– = =); barkat (= =) or, in the older Arabic reading, (– – =).

Handbook §2.3 ↗

Spelling that shows the scansion. Some words change their weight when their spelling changes, and are then scanned exactly as written: meraa (= x) versus miraa (– x); ek (= –) versus ik or yak (=); vahaañ (– x) versus vaañ (=). A tashdīd may also be present without being written, as in rakhaa: (– x) or (= x).

Handbook §2.4 ↗

Across word boundaries

The page shows separate words, but the voice runs some of them together. When a line seems a syllable too long or too short, look for a join: the iẓāfat, grafting, or the conjunction o.

ILM AL-ʿARŪḌ · METRICAL GEOMETRY

Khalil’s Circles & Meter Calculation

Khalil ibn Ahmad al-Farahidi (8th century CE) discovered that classical poetic meters are generated by five circular rhythmic loops. Rotating around the loop generates different base meters. Combining the rhythm with line length and ending modifications calculates the bahr’s full name and selects its classical verse.

THE FIVE METRICAL CIRCLES (الدَوَائِر العَرُوضِيَّة)

Starting Beat (Base Rhythm)

Line Length

Internal Foot Style (Body / Ḥashw)

Standard pristine feet or internal syllable softening (Khabn).

Final Foot Ending (Termination)

Sets how the final foot of the line concludes.

Why Poets Mix Sālim and Maḥẕūf in One Ghazal (The Scanner Sibling Rule)

Within a single ghazal, poets freely mix ziḥāf variations of the same base bahr. The first couplet might end intact (Sālim), while subsequent couplets trim the final foot (Maḥẕūf). Because both originate from the same circle rhythm, our scanner automatically recognizes and matches all permitted ziḥāf siblings of a bahr.

Scan a verse

Type or paste a verse in Urdu to see its bahr, syllable by syllable.

How to type for best results:

The script hides short vowels, so the scanner considers every plausible reading and lets the meter choose, like a reader would. Two things help it: write tashdīd ّ where a letter is doubled (مدّت، قصّہ، امّید), and write zer ِ for an iẓāfat you'd pronounce (غمِ دل). Everything else is automatic.

About Baḥr

Sources, scanner accuracy, and academic acknowledgments.

How far to trust the scanner

Tested against the handbook's own answer key: on all 24 exercise ghazals (226 lines), Pritchett's meter fits 225 lines, and stacking names the right meter for 23 of 24 ghazals (the miss: Akbar's English "M.A.", which she scans unusually). On her printed syllable-by-syllable breakdown of Mir's Hindi-meter ghazal it matches 108 of 108 syllables.

Rules: Pritchett & Khaliq, chs. 1–3. Word lists verified against the same.

The poets

Ghalib and Mir are Frances Pritchett's transcriptions. Every other poet in the Poets list comes from Rekhta↗, Sufinama↗ and Urdushahkar↗: the Urdu, Devanagari and Roman as given, with each ghazal linked to its source page. Rekhta, Sufinama and Urdushahkar do not name a ghazal's bahr, so the engine reads it from the poem: the meter family that fits most of its lines, using the Roman for what Urdu spelling hides (iẓāfat, doubled letters, a poet's pen name). A ghazal it cannot settle is listed as unfiled. The hand-checked and curated ghazals keep their verified Sean Pue transliteration.

Tips & Features

How to Use

Helpful features and controls you might not notice at first glance.

Sound & Rhythm Controls (⚙)

Tap the gear icon (⚙) in the top right to customize how poetry rhythms sound:

  • Voices: Switch between synthesized tabla strokes (dhā · tā), real recorded tabla, spoken human takes (dum / da), or clean pitch tones.
  • Record your own voice: Choose your voice in Settings to record yourself saying dum and da once — the app will play back rhythms in your own voice.
  • Tempo (BPM): Use the speed slider to slow down complex meters for careful listening or speed them up to natural recitation tempos.
  • Foot cues: Adjust the pause between metrical feet, or enable the soft drum pulse to feel where each metrical measure begins.

Interactive Scansion Tricks

  • Change a word's reading: In the Scan tab, tap any syllable chip to open its word: pin one of its alternate readings, add or remove an iẓāfat or tashdīd, or stop it grafting onto the next word. The line rescans at once.
  • Hear a broken line: If an edit (or a typo) knocks the misra out of meter, ▶︎ still plays it as typed. Dashed chips carry the wrong weight for the partner misra's bahr; chips marked extra have no place in it.
  • Live edits: Edit or tweak words directly in the scan box to see the meter matches and syllable chips update in real time.
  • No diacritics needed: You can paste transliterated poetry in plain Latin alphabet (e.g. dil e nadan) — the engine normalizes spelling and maps it to classical meter rules automatically.

Comparing Bahrs in Ghazals

  • Cross-poet comparison: In the Ghazals tab, poems are grouped by their bahr. Expand a group to see how Ghalib, Mir, and others built completely different moods inside the exact same rhythm.
  • Pattern vs. Verse: In any reader view, you can play the abstract meter pattern by itself or play the poem’s line to hear how words stretch and fit the beat.

Instant Script Switching

Use the اردو, हिन्दी, and Roman buttons in the header to switch scripts at any moment. Your active page, scanned couplet, and position are preserved instantly.

Shareable Direct Links

As you browse meters, search ghazals, or scan couplets, the URL in your browser address bar quietly updates with the relevant parameters (?open=, ?q=, ?t=). Copy and share the URL with anyone to take them straight to that exact meter, search, or scanned verse.

Tap

Make the rhythm with your own hand

Producing a rhythm trains the ear faster than hearing one. Tap once per syllable; hold a long twice as long as a short before the next tap.

Listen, then tap it back on the pad.

Recite a misra aloud and tap each syllable as you say it. Press Done when finished. I'll turn your taps into = and –, then check the bahr. The final syllable's length can't be heard from taps, so it stays flexible.
tap 

Practice

Whole lines, real poets. Tap the rhythm out yourself, or match a verse by ear.

Tap the rhythm, syllable by syllable

Say the line aloud. For each syllable press 1 if it is quick, 2 if it is held. When a foot is complete it will group together and play back. The names come at the end.
